power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: Background.
Impaired macrovascular function during acute mental stress predicts adverse events in coronary artery disease, but microvascular stress responses are less understood.
Because psychosocial stress and coronary microvascular dysfunction are more common in women, sex differences also warrant study.
We studied individuals aged 18-60 years within 8 months of a myocardial infarction (MI) who underwent a standardized mental stress challenge and were followed for cardiovascular events.
We measured peripheral microvascular function with the reactive hyperemia index (RHI) before and after stress; abnormal RHI was defined as ≤1.67.
We also measured brachial flow-mediated vasodilation (FMD), interleukin-6 (IL-6), and myocardial ischemia.
The primary endpoint was a composite of cardiovascular death, nonfatal MI, stroke, or heart failure hospitalization; a secondary endpoint included recurrent events.
Cox regression examined stress-induced RHI decline, adjusting for pre-stress RHI and demographic, clinical, and psychological factors.
Results.
Among 487 participants (mean age 51 years; 43% women), 89 first and 90 recurrent events occurred over a median 34 months.
Women had lower RHI than men before and after stress, and a larger stress-induced decline.

Each standard deviation stress-induced RHI decline was associated with 36% higher risk of first events (hazard ratio [HR], 1.36, 95% confidence interval [CI], 1.01, 1.82) and 44% higher risk of cumulative events (HR, 1.44, 95% CI, 1.04, 2.00), with no significant sex interaction.
Abnormal post-stress RHI conferred adjusted HRs of 2.59 (95% CI, 1.13, 5.92) in women and 2.09 (95% CI, 1.11, 3.93) in men; abnormal pre-stress RHI was not predictive (HR, 1.12, 95% CI, 0.71, 1.76).
IL-6 and FMD changes and stressinduced ischemia were related to RHI decline but did not explain its association with outcome.
Conclusions.
Microvascular dysfunction with mental stress is more prevalent in women, and signals an elevated cardiovascular risk after MI in both women and men.
What is already known on this topic -Macrovascular dysfunction in response to acute mental stress has been related to increased risk of recurrent events in people with coronary artery disease.
However, less is known about microvascular responses to stress.

What this study adds -A decline in microvascular function with mental stress is an independent predictor of subsequent cardiovascular events after a myocardial infarction (MI), and a stronger predictor than pre-stress microvascular function alone.
Women have worse resting microvascular function and a more adverse microvascular response to stress.
represent an important pathway linking psychological stress to adverse cardiovascular outcomes in people with MI.

The microvascular response to stress should be evaluated as a potentially modifiable marker of cardiovascular risk and intervention studies should determine whether targeting stress-related microvascular dysfunction can reduce cardiovascular risk in this population.

Decades of research have uncovered the contribution of psychological stress to cardiovascular physiology and the development and progression of cardiovascular disease. 1 In individuals with coronary artery disease (CAD), dynamic autonomic and molecular alterations during stress may help define cardiovascular risk. 2 Hemodynamic and vascular responses to laboratory stress, including changes in brachial artery flow-mediated vasodilation (FMD), predict long-term prognosis in CAD beyond pre-stress levels. 3 4 Less is known, however, about microvascular responses to stress, which may capture distinct pathophysiological pathways not reflected by macrovascular measures.

text.text: Peripheral arterial tonometry is a non-invasive method to evaluate peripheral microvascular function by measuring arterial pulsatile changes in the fingertip during post-occlusive reactive hyperemia. 5 The reactive hyperemia index (RHI) obtained with this device provides an estimate of peripheral microvascular vasodilator capacity that has been shown to predict cardiovascular events in individuals referred for evaluation to rule out CAD, patients with heart failure and those with stable CAD. 5 6 In an earlier, smaller wave of the Myocardial Infarction and Mental Stress (MIMS) study of young and middle-aged survivors of myocardial infarction (MI), stress-induced microvascular dysfunction predicted adverse events in women but not men. 7 With a limited number of outcome events, that analysis may have lacked sufficient statistical power to determine whether this association extends to men.

text.text: Here, leveraging the full MIMS sample across both recruitment waves, approximately doubling the number of participants and outcome events, we sought to examine whether the association between stress-induced peripheral microvascular dysfunction and adverse events after an MI generalizes to both sexes.

We also aimed to characterize the clinical and psychosocial correlates of stress-induced peripheral microvascular dysfunction, and to identify potential intervening factors that may explain its link to adverse outcomes.

The present analysis draws on data collected across two enrollment waves (Wave 2 and Wave 3) of the MIMS prospective cohort study. 8 9 Both waves employed consistent protocols that were established after an initial pilot phase (Wave 1).

text.text: Wave 2 recruited 313 individuals from April 2012 through March 2017; Wave 3 recruited 306 individuals from February 2020 through December 2023.
Core study procedures and laboratory methods remained unchanged across waves.

Participants were recruited from Emory University-affiliated hospitals in Atlanta and were 18 to 60 years of age with a hospital admission for Type 1 MI within the prior 8 months, confirmed by medical record review using standard criteria. 10 Exclusions included serious comorbid medical or psychiatric conditions, pregnancy or breastfeeding, immunosuppressive or nonantidepressant psychotropic medications, unstable cardiac conditions within 7 days, weight >450 lbs., and inability to safely withhold anti-ischemic medications for 24 hours.

text.text: Heart rate and blood pressure were recorded every 5 minutes at rest and every minute during the speech.

RHI was measured before and 30 minutes after mental stress with the Endo-PAT2000 device (Itamar Medical, Caesarea, Israel), which records finger pulse volume amplitude (PVA). 6 The reproducibility of RHI has been demonstrated before. 18 Reactive hyperemia was induced by 5-minute upper-arm cuff occlusion at 50 mm Hg above systolic pressure.

text.text: An automated algorithm derived the RHI as the ratio of post-deflation to baseline PVA in the occluded arm, normalized to the contralateral arm.
Lower RHI indicates worse function; following existing guidelines for clinical significance, a threshold of RHI ≤1.67 was used to define abnormal microvascular function. 19

text.text: Venous blood was drawn at rest and 90 minutes after stress, and plasma interleukin-6 (IL-6) was measured with a MesoScale Discovery electrochemiluminescence assay.

IL-6 is acutely 7 reactive to psychological stress, 21 particularly in younger women, 22 and has been associated with adverse cardiovascular outcomes in this population. 23 Assay precision was acceptable, with an inter-assay coefficient of variation of 5.8% and an intra-assay coefficient of variation of 3.3% for IL-6 midpoint standards.

Events were ascertained through participant contact, medical records, and death registries, and adjudicated by blinded cardiologists.

Sequential, a priori defined models, adjusted for pre-stress RHI (Model 1); then adding age, sex, and race (Model 2); then adding ever smoking, BMI, hypertension, diabetes, left ventricular ejection fraction, and ST-segment elevation MI (Model 3); and then adding depression and PTSD symptoms (Model 4).
Sensitivity analyses added marital status, education, medications, lifetime depression and PTSD, and perceived stress.

To illustrate the results, we plotted cumulative incidence curves according to presence or absence of abnormal post-stress RHI defined as RHI ≤1.67, in the overall population and by sex, adjusting for all variables in Model 4.

text.text: Analyses used SAS version 9.4 (SAS Inc., Cary, NC).
Of 619 MIMS participants, 487 (79%; 290 from Wave 2, 197 from Wave 3) had complete RHI data and formed the analytic sample.

RHI data were missing more in Wave 3 because of technical issues due to changes in equipment; also more in women (26% vs. 18%) and participants >50 years (23% vs. 18%), but missingness was unrelated to CAD risk factors or MI severity.

text.text: The sample included 209 women (43%); 59% self-identified as Black or African American, and mean age was 50.9 years (SD, 6.7).
Mean time since MI was 4.5 months (SD, 1.9).
The mean pre-stress RHI was 1.87 (SD, 0.59), and the mean post-stress RHI was 1.85 (SD, 0.63).
These metrics were approximately normally distributed.
Pre-stress RHI was moderately correlated with post-stress RHI and post-stress RHI decline (Spearman r=0.54 and r=0.37, respectively, p<0.001).

Of 219 participants with abnormal RHI poststress, 89 (41%) did not have an abnormal RHI pre-stress.
Women had lower RHI than men at rest (1.74 vs 1.93, p=0.01) and post-stress (1.73 vs.

Two participants could not be contacted at follow-up and therefore their follow-up time was censored shortly after the baseline visit.

text.text: The model was adjusted for prestress RHI, which was also significant (HR, 0.76, 95% CI, 0.59, 0.98, per SD), with higher prestress values being protective.

After adjustment for demographic and clinical factors, the association was slightly attenuated but significant (Model 3: HR, 1.38, 95% CI, 1.04, 1.84), whereas pre-stress RHI was no longer significant (HR, 0.88, 95% CI, 0.68, 1.14).
Adjustment for depression and PTSD symptoms had little effect on the estimate (Model 4: HR, 1.36, 95% CI, 1.01, 1.82).
Estimates were numerically larger in women, but sex interactions were not significant.

Recurrent event analyses yielded consistent, somewhat larger estimates (Table 4): each SD RHI decline was associated with 45% higher risk of first and recurrent events in Model 3 (HR, 1.45, 95% CI, 1.03, 2.04) and 44% higher risk of events in Model 4 (HR, 1.44, 95% CI, 1.04, 2.00).

text.text: Adjustment for stress-induced changes in FMD and IL-6 or for stressinduced ischemia did not materially change results, overall or by sex.

Among individuals recently hospitalized for an MI, a decline in microvascular function induced by mental stress measured by reactive hyperemia was related to an increase in MACE risk in an approximately linear fashion.

After adjusting for demographic, clinical and psychosocial factors, each SD decline of RHI post stress was associated with a 36% increased risk of incident MACE and 44% increased risk of incident and recurrent MACE over the followup.

Although estimates in women appeared larger and more consistently significant than those of men, especially in recurrent event analysis, there was no significant interaction by sex, suggesting that the risk of MACE associated with stress-induced RHI decline is relevant to both women and men.
An abnormal RHI post-stress, defined by a RHI value ≤1.67, was associated with over two-fold increased MACE risk both in women and in men.
By contrast, the association of pre-stress RHI with MACE was generally weaker and not statistically significant in this population.

These results suggest that microvascular dysfunction may be a pathway linking psychological stress to adverse cardiovascular outcomes in populations with a significant burden of CAD, such as after a MI.

Prior work by our group and independent investigators has demonstrated that RHI is predictive of adverse cardiovascular events in individuals with CAD. 6 29 However up to now, much less has been known on whether dynamic changes of RHI with acute mental stress exacerbate risk in post-MI individuals above and beyond pre-stress levels.

text.text: Women, however, had worse microvascular function before and after stress and a larger stress-induced decline, consistent with a high prevalence of microvascular dysfunction in women with suspected or established CAD than men, even without obstructive stenoses, and a more adverse microvascular response to stress. 30 Despite comprehensive measurements encompassing behavioral, physiological and clinical factors, we were unable to elucidate the mechanisms underlying the excess risk associated with stress-induced microvascular dysfunction.

text.text: An abnormal post-stress RHI was associated with a more adverse psychosocial risk profile, with a higher post-stress inflammatory response, with transient macrovascular dysfunction, and with a higher rate of mental stress induced ischemia.

However, none of these measures explained the risk associated with a decline in RHI with stress, suggesting a role for unmeasured biological or psychosocial mechanisms that should be the object of future studies.

The robust association between post-stress RHI decline and MACE underscores the importance of capturing the psychological domain in post-MI patients and has important implications for future research and clinical care.

The decline in RHI with laboratory mental stress may reflect susceptibility to stress-related microvascular dysregulation, which, if operative in daily life, could represent a mechanism linking chronic stress exposure to cardiovascular risk. 31 Advances in mobile health technologies may soon enable the unobtrusive, continuous collection of extensive physiological data alongside real-world daily experiences, including ambulatory monitoring of hemodynamic, vascular, and autonomic function.

text.text: Future large-scale prospective studies leveraging these technologies could help elucidate the mechanisms linking stress-induced microvascular dysfunction to subsequent cardiovascular events among patients recovering from an MI, and facilitate the validation and delivery of stress-reduction interventions.

For example, there is emerging evidence that autonomic modulation using heart rate variability biofeedback can increase myocardial blood flow during mental stress compared with usual care. 32 Although HRV was similar by RHI status in our study, this does not exclude sympathetic dysregulation, as HRV is an indirect measure of sympathetic activity. 25 Strengths of this study include a racially diverse sample with many women, comprehensive assessments, excellent retention, and blinded event adjudication.

text.text: Limitations include potential residual confounding and missing RHI data in 21% of participants, more often women, which may have led to underestimation of sex differences; however, missingness was unrelated to MI severity.
Multiple tests were performed, although all were prespecified.
We used a single stressor because sequential stressors may have cumulative effects, and a single stressor is necessary when using myocardial perfusion imaging with 99m Tc.
Furthermore, whether the laboratory stressor used in our study generalizes to real-world stress exposures is an important constraint on interpretation.

The single-center design with geographic concentration in Atlanta may limit the generalizability, but the diversity of the sample is a strength for generalizability 14 relative to many post-MI cohorts.

In conclusion, microvascular dysfunction in response to mental stress signals an elevated 329 risk of subsequent cardiovascular events in women and men after an MI, independent of 330 measured sociodemographic, psychosocial and clinical characteristics.

These findings 331 underscore the importance of considering the microvascular response to stress as a potentially 332 modifiable marker of cardiovascular risk in post-MI patients and highlight the need for 333 intervention studies to determine whether targeting stress-related microvascular dysfunction can 334 reduce this excess risk.
